Hypertension in an Adult

baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates them

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Confirm persistent blood pressure (BP) elevation, then assess organ injury, cardiovascular risk and comorbidities.
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on the ECG is established organ injury: do not delay indicated pressure treatment for an echo or stress test.
  • Resistant or young-onset hypertension, hypokalemia or a suggestive examination warrants a secondary-cause evaluation; renin separates primary aldosteronism from renovascular disease.
What it is

Sustained elevation of resting systolic or diastolic pressure, often without symptoms.

Driver

Primary hypertension has no single established cause; secondary hypertension has an identifiable disorder.

Triggers

Inherited susceptibility interacts with modifiable contributors: sodium intake, obesity or a sedentary lifestyle, and alcohol intake.

Chain

Increased vascular pressure and wall stress lead to cardiac hypertrophy and vascular or renal injury.

Insights

The comorbidity can select the drug: gout favors losartan; calcium stones or osteoporosis may favor a thiazide.

Hypokalemic alkalosis with hypertension suggests mineralocorticoid excess even if sodium is normal.

2Urgent risks
Acute injury versus chronic damage
FindingAction
Severe BP elevation with acute organ injuryEvaluate and treat as a hypertensive emergency. Chronic LVH alone is not the acute injury that defines an emergency.
Established LVH without an acute syndromeBegin indicated outpatient pressure treatment; further cardiac testing does not replace BP control.
3Differential
Secondary hypertension
CauseDecides itFirst test
Medication or substance effectCocaine or methamphetamine exposure; a corticosteroid, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or an oral contraceptive can also raise pressure.Review prescribed drugs, over-the-counter agents and substance exposure before attributing the pressure to a primary disorder.
Primary aldosteronism (primary hyperaldosteronism; Conn syndrome)Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; aldosterone elevated with renin suppressed.Measure an aldosterone-to-renin ratio.
Renal artery stenosis or fibromuscular dysplasiaRenovascular disease raises renin; unilateral renal artery stenosis can cause atrophy of the affected kidney. A young woman with an abdominal bruit suggests fibromuscular dysplasia.Order renal artery duplex or CT angiography as appropriate.
PheochromocytomaSpells of hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating.Measure plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines.
Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity, often with resistant hypertension.Obtain a sleep study; polysomnography can confirm the diagnosis.
Coarctation of the aortaDelayed or weak femoral pulses and higher arm than leg pressure; rib notching can support the diagnosis.Measure arm-leg pressures and obtain echocardiography or angiographic imaging.
Cushing syndromeCentral obesity, wide striae, proximal weakness and glucose or potassium abnormalities; mood and sleep symptoms may coexist.Screen cortisol production with an appropriate suppression, urine or salivary test.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Renin suppressedPrimary aldosteronismContinue the aldosterone workup.
Renin elevated with a renal artery lesionRenovascular hypertensionOrder renal artery duplex or CT angiography; angiotensin II mediates vasoconstriction.
Normal sodium despite mineralocorticoid excessAldosterone escape can limit sodium retentionDo not exclude primary aldosteronism because sodium is normal.
New mood or sleep symptoms with proximal weakness, central obesity and metabolic abnormalitiesCortisol excess rather than a primary mood disorder aloneMeasure 24-hour urinary free cortisol, one accepted initial screen, before assigning a primary psychiatric cause.
Pause point
Excess aldosterone and an adrenal nodule Read as proof of the producing gland A nodule shows anatomy → It does not by itself prove which gland is producing aldosterone
5Diagnostic criteria

Hypertension is sustained systolic pressure 130 mm Hg or more, diastolic pressure 80 mm Hg or more, or both. Confirm routine outpatient hypertension with ambulatory monitoring (preferred) or home readings before treatment.

6Severity
Initial drug count once treatment is indicated
BP categoryAction
Below 140/90 mm HgA single first-line agent can be used; choose it by comorbidity.
140/90 mm Hg or moreUsually begin a pair of different first-line agents; a fixed combination tablet can simplify the regimen.
7Treatment
1

InitialNo selecting comorbidity

Choose an ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB). In Black adults without a compelling renal or cardiac indication, a thiazide or dihydropyridine CCB is favored.

2

ComorbidityHypertension with a comorbidity

Choose an agent that also treats the relevant comorbidity.

3

CautionBilateral renal artery stenosis or additive rate-slowing drugs

ACE inhibition can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) when severe bilateral renal artery stenosis threatens filtration. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. Do not routinely combine a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem because of bradycardia, heart block and depressed contractility.

Antihypertensive choice
ConditionPreferred approach
GoutFavor losartan when possible; avoid hydrochlorothiazide when a suitable alternative exists.
Albuminuric chronic kidney diseaseUse an ACE inhibitor or ARB; monitor potassium and renal function.
Osteoporosis or calcium kidney stonesA thiazide reduces urinary calcium; it may help bone loss and recurrent calcium stones.
MigraineA beta-blocker can treat both hypertension and migraine prophylaxis.
Atrial fibrillation or flutterUse a beta-blocker or a nondihydropyridine CCB for rate control as appropriate; avoid the latter in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Coronary disease
Reduced-fraction heart failure
8Follow-up
Monitoring
SituationDo
About 1 month after starting or adjusting therapyReassess BP, adherence, adverse effects and the relevant renal or electrolyte results.
Persistent hypertension despite treatmentReassess the regimen and evaluate a secondary cause when indicated by the clinical pattern.
Mineralocorticoid physiologyExplains the potassium and renin pattern
Collecting ductAldosterone increases epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) activity; sodium uptake promotes potassium and hydrogen secretion.Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis can result.
Aldosterone escapeAtrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and pressure natriuresis limit retained sodium.Clinically significant edema or hypernatremia is usually absent in primary aldosteronism.
Renal artery stenosisReduced renal perfusion activates renin and angiotensin II.Angiotensin II both constricts vessels and supports glomerular filtration rate (GFR) when perfusion is compromised.

The drug-selection cases below assume persistent hypertension has been confirmed with out-of-office readings. If confirmation is the question, obtain ambulatory or home measurements before routine outpatient treatment.

Practice
  1. 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL → Losartan → gout picks losartan, which is mildly uricosuric; a thiazide raises urate, and stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the hypertrophy
  2. 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide lowers blood pressure and may attenuate bone loss by reducing urinary calcium loss; losartan and a dihydropyridine CCB lack this calcium-conserving benefit
  3. 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L → ACE inhibitor → albuminuric chronic kidney disease takes an ACE inhibitor or ARB; a thiazide or a nondihydropyridine CCB treats only the pressure
  4. 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min → Beta-blocker → a beta-blocker treats both the pressure and the migraine, one drug for both diagnoses; a thiazide treats only the pressure, and hydralazine is not a first-line class
  5. 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium and treats both; a loop diuretic increases urinary calcium, and losartan treats only the pressure
  6. 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Start an antihypertensive now → left ventricular hypertrophy is end-organ injury, the treatment gate; echo or stress testing only characterizes it and never delays the first drug
  7. 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Aldosterone-to-renin ratio → hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function are mineralocorticoid excess; a suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease, and a normal sodium (aldosterone escape) does not argue against it. Duplex fits a bruit, metanephrines fit spells
  8. 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Fibromuscular dysplasia → a young woman with an abdominal bruit and high renin has fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, a disease of the media): CT angiography. Primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; coarctation weakens the femoral pulses
  9. 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min → Pheochromocytoma → episodic hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating is pheochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines, several-fold high, then adrenal CT or MRI. A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone argues against hyperthyroidism, and panic disorder is not diagnosed when another condition better explains the spells
  10. 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg → Coarctation of the aorta → weak femoral pulses, rib notching and an arm-leg pressure gradient are coarctation of the aorta; CT or magnetic resonance angiography defines the narrowing. Renal artery stenosis does not explain weak femoral pulses, rib notching or an arm-leg gradient, and pheochromocytoma commonly brings episodic headaches, sweating and a racing heart, and he has neither sweating nor palpitations
  11. 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L → Obstructive sleep apnea → snoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity with resistant hypertension are obstructive sleep apnea: polysomnography, itself the confirmatory test. Snoring, sleepiness and a thick neck point to the airway first, and there are no striae to suggest Cushing syndrome
  12. 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL → Cushing syndrome → striae, moon facies and hyperglycemia are Cushing syndrome: an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, then a second, different screening test, then ACTH to localize
  13. 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed → Adrenal venous sampling → An adrenal nodule identifies anatomy but not autonomous hormone production. Adrenal venous sampling lateralizes aldosterone secretion before unilateral surgery in most candidates.
  14. 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL → An ACE inhibitor → the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR, so with bilateral lesions an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated: it can cause AKI; a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide are effective at controlling pressure in renal artery stenosis
  15. 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL → Angiotensin II → renin initiates the cascade and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia, but angiotensin II directly mediates the vasoconstriction
Common wrong answers Discontinue the allopurinol: stopping it treats neither the pressure nor the LVH. Echo or stress testing first: characterizing injury does not replace indicated blood-pressure treatment.
Pairs with Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: fibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient. Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child: low potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status.
Transferable rule

Match the drug to the comorbidity. Biochemical testing establishes primary aldosteronism; imaging defines adrenal anatomy. For most surgical candidates, adrenal venous sampling is needed to identify unilateral secretion; an adrenal nodule alone does not establish a functional adenoma.
